steps.say: CPAM tops the list of newborn lung lumps, though most parents will never meet one. It affects 1 in 25000 to 35000 births as a multicystic hamartoma from blocked airway branching. The faulty segment keeps its bronchial connection and fills with air on a pulmonary blood supply.
steps.tx: **CPAM** (congenital pulmonary airway malformation) is the most common congenital lung lesion at 1 in **25000** to **35000** births, a multicystic **hamartoma** (jumbled tissue overgrowth) from **pseudoglandular phase** (mid pregnancy airway branching) obstruction. It communicates with the bronchial tree on pulmonary blood supply.

steps.say: Many of these lung shadows melt away before delivery, so serial scans are bringing good news in most pregnancies. Antenatal betamethasone shrinks large lesions and can reverse hydrops in the swollen fetus. Only severe compression with hydrops needs in utero needling or shunting.
steps.tx: Many prenatal lesions show **prenatal regression** (third trimester shrinkage), and antenatal **betamethasone** (steroid shrinking lesions) reverses **hydrops** (fetal fluid swelling). Severe fetal compression with hydrops may need in utero intervention, while regressing lesions are watched to term. Steroids work best before hydrops becomes severe, so refer urgently to the fetal centre.

nodes.label: Betamethasone for large lesions and hydrops
Regression watched; severe compression treated in utero

steps.say: A grunting blue newborn with fast breathing may be showing a CPAM that filled with air at birth. Tachypnea, grunting and oxygen need mark the symptomatic baby. Older children instead return with recurrent pneumonia, pneumothorax, bleeding or lung abscess in the same lobe.
steps.tx: Symptomatic newborns show tachypnea, grunting and oxygen need with **respiratory distress** (laboured newborn breathing), while older children present with **recurrent pneumonia** (same lobe infections), **pneumothorax** (collapsed lung air leak), hemoptysis or lung abscess. Ballooning cysts may also compress neighbours and mimic tension pneumothorax on films.

steps.say: The Stocker system replaced the old three type scheme because it predicts behaviour better. Five types from 0 to IV follow the airway level of origin with matching cyst content and scans. Macrocystic and microcystic patterns sit inside this map rather than standing alone.
steps.tx: The **Stocker classification** (five types **0** to **IV** by airway origin) stages cyst content and radiology, replacing the old **macrocystic** (big cyst), mixed and solid three type scheme. **Microcystic** (tiny cyst) disease maps to higher types with worse outlook and clearer surgical planning.

steps.say: Leaving the lesion invites infection and a small cancer risk, while removing it lets the remaining lung grow. Resect every affected child within the first 2 years of life. Early lobectomy prevents infection, allows compensatory lung growth and removes malignant potential.
steps.tx: Resection is advised in every child without spontaneous regression within the first **2** years of life. Early **surgical resection** (lobe removal) prevents infection, allows compensatory **lung growth** (remaining lung expansion) and removes **malignant transformation** (later cancer in the cyst wall).

steps.say: A plain film starts the workup, but cross sectional scans are separating lookalike lesions before surgery. Chest radiography is showing cysts or pneumothorax in the newborn. Computed tomography or magnetic resonance then distinguishes CPAM from sequestration and diaphragmatic hernia.
steps.tx: Postnatal workup uses **chest radiograph** (plain film showing cysts or pneumothorax) plus **computed tomography** (CT mapping cysts) or magnetic resonance to separate CPAM in the **differential diagnosis** (sequestration versus diaphragmatic hernia list) from lookalikes. Doppler flow studies confirm which vessel feeds the lesion before the surgeon operates.

vis.alt: Intralobar sequestration sharing visceral pleura with pulmonary venous drainage beside extralobar sequestration with systemic venous drainage.
vis.caption: Doppler and CT separate CPAM with pulmonary supply from sequestration with systemic supply. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A squeezed lung cannot breathe, so a flat blue baby with shifted heart sounds needs instant action. Severe asphyxia from compression and mediastinal shift defeats bag ventilation. Emergency resection or ECMO bypasses the crushed lung until it can inflate.
steps.tx: Severe birth asphyxia from lung compression and **mediastinal shift** (heart pushed across) with **pulmonary hypoplasia** (undergrown compressed lung) needs **emergency resection** (immediate lobe removal) or ECMO, since the compressed lung cannot ventilate. Ventilation fails because air cannot enter the squashed lung despite high pressures.

vis.alt: Infant diagrams showing diaphragmatic hernia with pulmonary hypoplasia beside covered omphalocele and uncovered gastroschisis.
vis.caption: Compression with mediastinal shift and pulmonary hypoplasia needs emergency resection or ECMO. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The story starts on the antenatal scan, where a bright lung wedge flags the lesion months early. Prenatal ultrasound with fetal magnetic resonance tracks size and hydrops through pregnancy. Doppler plus postnatal imaging then defines the systemic versus pulmonary blood supply before surgery.
steps.tx: CPAM shares prenatal ultrasound and **fetal magnetic resonance** (womb MRI tracking size) detection with sequestration, and **Doppler** (flow ultrasound) plus postnatal imaging defines the **blood supply** (systemic versus pulmonary feeding vessels) that separates the two lesions. Lesions that vanish by birth still need one postnatal scan to confirm complete resolution.

nodes.label: Fetal resonance tracks size and hydrops
Doppler defines systemic or pulmonary supply
